newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia welcomes PNG climbdown on mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: Australia welcomes PNG climbdown on mercenaries.

text.p: Australia on Friday welcomed Papua New Guinea's suspension of a US$28 million mercenary contract and urged the immediate departure of the hired guns to help restore peace to the South Pacific nation.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer backed Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan's decision to suspend the contract with Sandline International in the face of civil and military opposition which has swept the impoverished country.
"I hope to see Sandline on aircraft out of Papua New Guinea and as soon as possible," Downer told Australian radio.

"It's obviously a positive development and so we see it as welcome news. But it's important that this development is followed by a return to calm and that the civil authority is able to prevail in Port Moresby."
Australia's top diplomat, despatched to Port Moresby on an emergency mission by Prime Minister John Howard, was due to resume talks with Chan on Friday to help resolve the crisis.

Australia was the colonial administrator of New Guinea before independence in 1975 and retains close ties. Australia is the country's largest aid donor and Australian investments are seen as vital to its economy.

Protesters and soldiers on Thursday continued to demand Chan's resignation over his plan to use the mercenaries to help quell a secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island, 800 kilometres (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.

Stung by the unrest, Chan said on Thursday an inquiry would be held into the deal with British-based Sandline and the contract suspended pending its outcome. The mercenaries have already begun to leave Papua New Guinea.

Australia has offered what it calls reasonable and practical alternatives to the mercenary strategy, reportedly including increased training for the ill-equipped and poorly-trained Papua New Guinea military.
Howard's envoy, Foreign Affairs Department chief Philip Flood, was discussing Australia's offers with Chan.
"We've made some offers of practical alternatives to what has been going on in recent times and we are continuing to do that," Downer said.

The crisis began on Monday when defence chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded Chan quit and an inquiry be held into the hiring of Sandline. Protesters and troops are demanding that Singirok is reinstated.
